en: The Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time,
the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“A wheel-turning sage king possesses these four unprecedented qualities.”
What are the four?
In this regard, the Wheel-Turning Sage King loves and cherishes all his subjects, never harming them, just as a father loves his son;

the Wheel-Turning Sage King is likewise, loving and respecting his people and never showing them anger, just as a father has an only son. This is called the first unprecedented quality of the Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King travels among the people, they all rejoice upon seeing him as a child does toward a loving father; this is called the second extraordinary quality of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King remains stationary and does not travel, all among the populace who behold him attain joy; that Wheel-Turning Sage King preaches the Dharma to the people, and all who hear it likewise attain joy. At that time, the people never tire of hearing the Wheel-Turning Sage King preach the Dharma; this is called the third extraordinary quality of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King sits and does not travel about, all the people who behold him are filled with joy. That Wheel-Turning Sage King instructs the people: "This should be done; this should not be done. This is to be associated with; this is not to be associated with. If one performs such deeds, one will obtain inexhaustible merit for a long night; if one performs such deeds, one will suffer for a long night without respite. When those people hear such instructions from the Wheel-Turning Sage King, they rejoice without satiety. This is called the unprecedented quality possessed by the Wheel-Turning Sage King.
“In this way, Ānanda the bhikṣu also possesses four extraordinary qualities.
What are these four?

In this regard, whenever the bhikṣu Ānanda enters among the assembly of bhikṣus, all the bhikṣus who see him are filled with joy; when that bhikṣu Ānanda preaches the Dharma for them, all those who hear the Dharma are likewise filled with joy; and the bhikṣus never tire of hearing what Ānanda says. This is called the first extraordinary quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda.”

If the bhikṣu Ānanda goes silently into the midst of the community of bhikṣuṇīs, all who see him are filled with joy; when that bhikṣu Ānanda preaches the Dharma for them, those who hear the Dharma all attain joy. At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs never tires of hearing Ānanda preach the Dharma. This is called the second extraordinary quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if he goes silently to the place of the upāsakas, the upāsakas rejoice upon seeing him; that bhikṣu Ānanda then preaches the Dharma for them, and the assembly of upāsakas never tires of hearing what Ānanda says. This is called the third extraordinary quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda.

Furthermore, Ānanda the bhikṣu would silently approach the assembly of upāsikās; all who saw him were filled with joy, and as he preached the Dharma for them, the upāsikās never grew weary of listening. These are called the four extraordinary qualities of the bhikṣu Ānanda.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented Dharmas* translated above: the title and the name of the translator are identical in all the various canons; furthermore, the textual meaning of both the Northern (Dan) and Song editions is entirely the same. From beginning to end, this sūtra speaks exclusively of the merit of constructing stūpas; although it concludes by naming these as "unprecedented dharmas," throughout the entire text there is not the meaning of the four [unprecedented] dharmas. This Dan edition of the sūtra, however, explains that a Cakravartin King possesses four unprecedented dharmas, using them as a metaphor for Ānanda’s possession of four unprecedented dharmas as well.

According to the *Kaiyuan lu*, within the "Ruò" (若) fascicle there is the *Catvāry-āścaryādbhuta-sūtra*, which is said to be a different translation of the same original text as the "Eight Difficulties Chapter" (*Aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Now, upon examining the Danben (Dan-zang edition), it is indeed this very text;

whereas the Songben (Song-zang edition) of this scripture is simply the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya* found within the previous "Destruction" (Huǐ) case, translated during the Later Han with the translator's name lost and recorded in ancient catalogs.

It appears that the Song edition of the canon, within this "Ruò" (若) fascicle, lost the authentic *Sì wèicéngyǒu jīng* (Four Sūtras on the Unprecedented) and instead obtained the *Wèicéngyǒu jīng* from the "Huǐ" (毀) fascicle; taking it to be a case where four characters were omitted from the title, it subsequently added those four characters and recompiled it here—this is an error.
Alas! There are four errors in this mistake:
first, the loss of the authentic *Catur-āścaryādbhuta-sūtra*;...
First, this single volume of the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* is recorded twice;
second, it was originally a work of lost translation that was later translated by Dharmarakṣa;
third, although it is a Mahāyāna text, it has been suppressed and included within this Śrāvaka Piṭaka; and fourth, [it contains internal contradictions].

Therefore, I have omitted the Song edition and adopted the Dan edition. If later scholars wish to know what kind of passages were omitted here, they should consult the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* in the "Hui" (Destruction) case; it is precisely there.
